script.opening: "Thanks for seeing me. It’s honestly probably nothing — I’ve just been getting really dizzy when I stand up, and a bit faint at school, and I’m tired all the time. I think I’m just run down with exams and maybe a bit anaemic? Could I just get some iron tablets or a blood test? I’ve actually been really good with eating healthily and exercising, so I don’t get why I feel so rubbish."

facts.text: If asked: dizziness/syncope on standing (suggesting a postural drop), cold intolerance, fatigue, amenorrhoea 4 months, rapid significant weight loss, clothes much looser. None of this can be measured on a video call; at a same-day in-person assessment the markers of risk would include: bradycardia, postural hypotension, low BMI, cold peripheries, possibly lanugo. These are MEDICAL instability markers — an eating disorder can be physically dangerous, not just psychological.

If gently explored: severe dietary restriction, calorie/macros obsession, compulsive exercise (hours daily, distress if prevented), intense fear of weight gain, body-image distortion (feels "huge" despite being underweight). She reframes all of it as "clean eating" and discipline. Likely anorexia nervosa.

HIDDEN AGENDA — she did NOT come to talk about eating; she came for a fix for the dizziness (iron/bloods) precisely so she can keep functioning and keep restricting. Underneath is terror of losing control and of being "made to gain weight", plus the eating disorder serving as control amid overwhelming academic and family perfectionism pressure. She will minimise hard and may become defensive if confronted bluntly.

If reached: huge pressure to achieve (parental expectations, top set), the restriction is the one thing she feels in control of; deep shame; possibly low mood. The "I’m just being healthy" is both genuine distortion and a shield.

Officially: iron tablets / a blood test to fix the dizziness. What she needs: recognition of an eating disorder with potentially dangerous medical instability, a non-judgemental opening of the subject, assessment of medical risk in person the same day (RCPsych MEED, CR233, 2022), and immediate referral (NICE NG69) — engaged gently so she doesn’t flee.

ice.ideas: She’s just run down / anaemic from exams and needs iron or a blood test; her eating is "healthy".
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — terror of losing control and of being "made to gain weight"; the restriction is her coping/control amid perfectionist pressure; she wants the dizziness fixed so she can keep going, not the eating addressed.
ice.expectations: Iron tablets or a blood test. What she actually needs: recognition of an eating disorder and its medical danger, a gentle opening of the subject, medical-risk assessment, and urgent referral.

cues: "I’ve been really good with eating healthily and exercising" + faint/dizzy + thin in layers — the eating disorder reframed as discipline.
Dizziness on standing, cold, periods stopped, rapid weight loss — medical instability, not simple anaemia.
Defensiveness or a flicker if eating/weight is mentioned — the fear of losing control; approach gently, not bluntly.

checkpoints.text: Recognises the picture as a probable EATING DISORDER (restriction, compulsive exercise, fear of weight gain, body-image distortion, amenorrhoea, rapid weight loss) rather than accepting "run down/anaemic" and simply ordering iron — and does not collude with the "healthy eating" framing

Recognises that medical risk CANNOT be assessed on a video call and arranges a SAME-DAY IN-PERSON assessment (RCPsych MEED, CR233, 2022: primary care assesses in person and seeks collateral from family, as patients often minimise): lying and standing pulse and BP (postural drop, bradycardia), weight, BMI and rate of weight loss, hydration, ability to rise (sit-up–squat–stand), temperature — and recognises these can indicate a medical emergency, not just a mental-health issue (red MEED features = same-day medical admission)

Opens the eating subject GENTLY and non-judgementally (e.g. "lots of people under big pressure find their relationship with food changes — can I ask how you’ve been feeling about eating and your body?") so she does not become defensive and disengage

Arranges appropriate investigation and URGENT referral: bloods including FBC, U&E, phosphate, magnesium, calcium, glucose and LFTs, and an ECG (NICE NG69: assess the need for ECG monitoring with rapid weight loss, excessive exercise, bradycardia or hypotension; refeeding awareness), and immediate referral to a community, age-appropriate eating-disorder service (NICE NG69), marked urgent (NHS England CYP eating disorder standard, 2015: urgent cases start treatment within 1 week) — with same-day/emergency escalation if medically unstable per MEED

Explores the psychological and contextual drivers (perfectionism, academic/family pressure, control, low mood, shame) and screens mood/self-harm risk, without making the first consultation a confrontation
Builds trust with a minimising, frightened young person: validates the distress under the control, avoids weight/food battles or alarm that would push her away, and conveys care rather than judgement

Handles confidentiality and family involvement appropriately for her age and risk (GMC 0–18 years) — explaining that her safety means some sharing, done with her, while respecting her as far as possible

Safety-nets and coordinates: explains why this is being taken seriously medically, arranges urgent CEDS referral and monitoring, gives red flags (collapse, chest pain, palpitations → urgent), involves family/school appropriately, and books close follow-up

worked.txt: "I’m really glad you came about the dizziness, because it IS your body telling us something important — and I want to take it properly seriously rather than just hand you iron tablets. I can’t check what I need to over video, so I’d like you to come in today: your pulse and blood pressure lying and standing, your temperature and your weight tell me a lot about what’s going on. Can someone bring you?"

"Here’s what I’m hearing: you’re dizzy when you stand, you’re cold all the time, your weight has dropped fast and your periods have stopped. Together those tell me your body isn’t getting enough fuel — and when I see you today I’ll check whether your heart is running slow or your blood pressure drops when you stand, and that can become genuinely dangerous — not in a telling-off way, in a ‘your body is struggling and I want to protect you’ way."

"Can I ask you something gently? A lot of people — especially bright, driven people under huge pressure — find that eating and exercise become one of the few things they can control, and it can tip into restricting more than the body can cope with. Does any of that feel familiar? There’s zero judgement here."

"If I’ve understood right, with all the exam and achievement pressure, controlling food and exercise is the one area that feels like yours. That makes complete sense, and it’s not vanity or attention — it’s a way of coping with something overwhelming. The problem is it’s started to put your body in real danger, and that’s what we have to look after."

"So I’m not going to just do a blood test and send you off. I do want bloods and a heart tracing today when you come in, because the salts in your blood and your heart need checking. And I want to refer you straight away, marked urgent, to a team who specialise in exactly this — not because you’re in trouble, but because you deserve proper support and because your body needs it. This is treatable, and people do recover."

"Because you’re 16 and because your safety matters, the people who care about you will need to be part of this — but we’ll talk about how that’s done together, and I’ll keep you involved. If you feel faint and actually pass out, get chest pain or your heart racing, that’s urgent help straight away. I’m going to see you again very soon. You came in feeling rubbish and hoping for a quick fix — what you’re getting is people who are going to help you properly."

f.learning: Dizziness, faints, fatigue, cold intolerance and amenorrhoea in a thin, high-achieving teenager presenting for "iron tablets" is an eating disorder until proven otherwise — and the dizziness is the door, not the diagnosis. The critical clinical task is recognising that eating disorders carry potentially dangerous MEDICAL instability: a video call cannot assess it, so arrange a same-day in-person assessment of lying and standing pulse/BP (bradycardia, postural drop), weight, BMI and rate of loss, ability to rise, temperature (RCPsych MEED, CR233, 2022), with collateral from family, and arrange bloods (FBC, U&E, phosphate, magnesium, calcium, glucose, LFTs) and an ECG (NICE NG69) with refeeding awareness, escalating to same-day admission if red MEED features. The examinable hidden agenda is that she came to fix the dizziness so she can keep restricting; underneath is terror of losing control and being "made to gain weight", with the disorder serving as control amid perfectionist pressure. Open the subject gently (never bluntly or with food/weight battles), validate the distress and control without colluding with "healthy eating", refer immediately to the community eating-disorder service (NICE NG69; NHS England CYP standard: urgent cases start treatment within 1 week), handle family involvement by age and risk, and safety-net. Confrontation makes her flee; warmth with honesty keeps her.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG69 (eating disorders, 2017, updated 2020) · RCPsych CR233 Medical emergencies in eating disorders (MEED, 2022) · NHS England CYP eating disorder access and waiting time standard (2015) · GMC 0–18 years (2007)
knowledge.summary: Postural dizziness, faints, cold intolerance, amenorrhoea and rapid weight loss in a thin, driven teenager asking for iron is an eating disorder until proven otherwise — and a possible medical emergency. She needs an in-person physical risk assessment the same day and an immediate referral.

points.t: Restriction, calorie counting, hours of exercise, fear of weight gain, body-image distortion, rapid weight loss and amenorrhoea point to anorexia nervosa. Framing it as “healthy eating” is part of the illness, not evidence against it.

RCPsych MEED (CR233, 2022) covers all ages and uses a red, amber and green risk system: degree and rate of weight loss, heart rate, lying and standing blood pressure and pulse, temperature, hydration, the sit-up–squat–stand test, blood results and ECG. It advises that primary care assesses these in person and seeks collateral from family, as patients often minimise.

FBC, U&E, phosphate, magnesium, calcium, glucose, LFTs. NICE NG69: assess the need for ECG monitoring with rapid weight loss, excessive exercise, bradycardia, hypotension, electrolyte imbalance or muscular weakness — several of which apply. Normal bloods do not exclude danger.

NICE NG69: if an eating disorder is suspected after initial assessment, refer immediately to a community-based, age-appropriate eating disorder service. Do not use a single measure such as BMI or duration of illness to decide whether to offer treatment. One red or two or more amber MEED features need urgent same-day discussion with the acute paediatric and eating disorder teams; admit if she cannot be stabilised safely in the community.

NHS England standard (2015) for children and young people: treatment in line with NICE NG69 should start within 1 week for urgent cases and within 4 weeks for routine cases. Mark this referral urgent.

NICE NG69: consider anorexia-nervosa-focused family therapy for children and young people, with some appointments seen separately from family. Do not offer medication as the sole treatment. Family involvement is part of treatment, negotiated with her.

dg.d: Open question; took the faints seriously without accepting “just anaemia” and agreed a wider agenda.
Academic and parental pressure, perfectionism, need for control, mood and self-harm screen.
Same-day in-person lying and standing BP and pulse, temperature, weight, sit-up–squat–stand; FBC, U&E, phosphate, magnesium, glucose, LFTs; ECG (MEED, NICE NG69).
Anorexia nervosa vs anaemia, thyroid disease, coeliac disease and other causes of weight loss; cardiac causes of presyncope.
Asked about blackouts, chest pain and palpitations; recognised postural symptoms and rapid weight loss as possible medical instability.
Probable anorexia nervosa with possible medical instability, explained as an illness rather than a choice.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Same-day physical assessment with admission if red MEED features; immediate urgent referral to the community eating disorder service.
Low mood screened; exam pressure acknowledged; family involvement negotiated; exercise paused today.
999 for collapse, chest pain, palpitations or weakness; seen today; review after results and once the team is involved.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

Idea (run down, anaemic), concern (being made to gain weight, losing control), expectation (iron or a blood test).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — terror of losing control and of being "made to gain weight"; the restriction is her coping/control amid perfectionist pressure; she wants the dizziness fixed so she can keep going, not the eating addressed — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hi Ivy, I’m Dr Lee. Thanks for booking in. Tell me what’s been going on.
model.why: Open question, letting her set out her story

model.text: It’s probably nothing. I get really dizzy when I stand up, a bit faint at school, and I’m tired all the time. I think I’m run down with exams, maybe anaemic? Could I just get iron or a blood test? I’ve been really good with eating healthily and exercising, so I don’t get why I feel so rubbish.

I’m glad you came, because fainting at school is something I want to take properly seriously, not just give you tablets for. Can I ask you some questions to work out what’s behind it, and then we’ll decide on tests together?
model.why: Validates the symptom and agrees an agenda wider than iron

model.text: Okay.
Tell me about the faints. Have you actually blacked out? Any chest pain, heart racing or fluttering?
Not fully blacked out. Everything goes grey when I stand. No chest pain.
You mentioned eating healthily and exercising. What does a typical day look like — food and exercise?
model.why: Uses her own words to open the subject non-confrontationally

model.text: Clean eating. I track everything. I train a couple of hours a day — running, workouts. It’s just discipline.
How do you feel if you can’t train, or eat more than you planned?
model.why: Tests for compulsive exercise and fear of weight gain

model.text: (Pause.) Awful. Like I’ve failed. I feel huge, honestly, even though people say I’m thin.
Thank you for being honest. Has your weight changed recently? And your periods — are they regular?
model.why: Establishes rapid weight loss and amenorrhoea

model.text: I’ve lost quite a bit, quite fast. My periods stopped about four months ago. I thought that was stress.
And your mood — how have you been in yourself? Any thoughts of harming yourself?
Stressed. Low sometimes. Nothing like that.
It sounds like there’s a lot of pressure on you right now. What’s that like?
model.why: Explores context and control without challenging her

model.text: My parents expect top grades. I’m in all the top sets. Food’s the one thing I can actually control.
That makes a lot of sense. When everything feels like it’s about performing, having one thing that’s yours matters. What worries you most about what I might say today?
model.why: Validates the need for control and elicits her fear

model.text: (Quietly.) That you’ll make me gain weight. That I’ll lose control.

Thank you for telling me that. I’ll be honest with you. Losing weight fast, periods stopping, feeling cold, going grey when you stand — those tell me your body isn’t getting enough fuel for what you’re asking of it. I don’t think this is anaemia. I think your eating and exercise have become an eating disorder, and it’s started to affect your heart and blood pressure.
model.why: Names the probable eating disorder and its medical danger, gently

model.text: I’m not ill. I’m just being healthy.

I can see why it feels that way — it started as trying to be healthy. But being healthy shouldn’t make you faint. This isn’t about blame or vanity; it’s an illness, it’s treatable, and people do recover. And I won’t make any decisions without you.
model.why: Avoids argument, reframes as illness and restores some control

model.text: …Okay.

Here’s what I’d like. I can’t check your heart properly over video, so I’d like you to come in today. We’ll check your pulse and blood pressure lying and standing, your temperature and weight, do a heart tracing and bloods for your salts and sugar. If anything is dangerous, you may need to be seen in hospital today.
model.why: Same-day in-person MEED risk assessment, bloods and ECG

model.text: Today? I’ve got revision.

I know exams matter a lot to you. Fainting could hurt you, and it will affect your revision far more than an hour here. I’ll also refer you urgently to the eating disorder team for young people — they’re specialists, and they aim to see urgent referrals within a week.
model.why: Urgent CEDS referral in line with NICE NG69 and the waiting time standard

model.text: Do my parents have to know?

Because this is affecting your physical safety, your family will need to be involved — the treatment that works best for people your age includes them. But we can decide together how, and what you’d like to say first. Would it help if I was there when you tell them?
model.why: Honest about limits of confidentiality at 16, negotiated with her

model.text: …Maybe. Mum, not Dad first.
That’s fine. Please come in this afternoon — can someone bring you? Until then, if you pass out, get chest pain, your heart races or you feel very weak, ring 999. Please don’t exercise today.
model.why: Same-day attendance and explicit emergency triggers

model.text: Before we finish, tell me in your own words what we’ve agreed.
Come in today for checks, bloods and a heart tracing. You’re referring me to a specialist team. We tell Mum together. 999 if I pass out or get chest pain.
Exactly. You came hoping for a quick fix, and I know this is harder to hear. You did the right thing coming, and you won’t be doing this alone.
model.why: Closes with warmth and acknowledges the gap between wish and plan

social.t: High academic and parental expectations often sit behind restriction as a means of control. Acknowledge exams as important to her while making clear that her safety comes first.
Family-based treatment is central for adolescents (NICE NG69). She may want one parent told first; honouring that preference where safe keeps her engaged.

legal.t: At 16 she is presumed to have capacity (Mental Capacity Act 2005) and can consent to treatment (Family Law Reform Act 1969, s8). Anorexia can impair capacity for decisions about food and weight; assess capacity for the specific decision.

GMC 0–18 years: information can be shared without consent where necessary to protect a young person from risk of death or serious harm. A medically unstable eating disorder can meet this threshold; involve her in how it is done.
If illness affects her exams, her school can apply for access arrangements or special consideration through the exam boards’ JCQ process.

professional.t: MEED advises in-person physical assessment in primary care. A video consultation can open the subject but cannot measure postural observations; arrange a same-day face-to-face review (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024: recognise the limits of the consultation).
Record the history, observations, MEED risk features, the referral and its urgency, and the confidentiality discussion.

community.t: Beat (UK eating disorder charity) for Ivy and her family; school pastoral team or school nurse, with her agreement; the community eating disorder service’s family support.

redFlags: Syncope, chest pain, palpitations or muscle weakness — urgent assessment
Rapid weight loss, bradycardia, postural drop, low temperature, failed sit-up–squat–stand — MEED red or amber features
Self-harm or suicidal thoughts; purging or laxative use
psychosocial: Perfectionism and parental expectations; top sets; A-levels
Food and exercise as the one area she controls
Shame and fear of being made to gain weight
ice: Idea: “I’m run down with exams — maybe anaemic.”
Concern: being made to gain weight and losing control
Expectation: iron tablets or a blood test

playbook.diagnosis: Probable anorexia nervosa (restriction, compulsive exercise, fear of weight gain, body-image distortion, rapid weight loss, 4 months’ amenorrhoea) with symptoms suggesting medical instability (postural presyncope, cold intolerance). Needs same-day in-person physical risk assessment.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Your body isn’t getting enough fuel for what you’re asking of it, so it’s slowing things down — that’s why you’re cold, your periods stopped and you go grey when you stand. That’s an eating disorder. It’s an illness, not a choice, and it can be treated.”

management.reflectIce: “You were hoping this was anaemia, and you’re frightened of being made to gain weight and losing control. I won’t make decisions without you, but I do need to keep you safe.”
management.psychosocial: Validate the pressure and need for control; avoid food and weight arguments; negotiate which parent is told first and how; involve school only with her agreement.
sharedPlan: Same-day in-person observations (lying and standing BP and pulse, temperature, weight, sit-up–squat–stand), bloods and ECG (MEED, NICE NG69)
Immediate urgent referral to the community eating disorder service (NICE NG69; NHS England standard, urgent within 1 week)
Same-day medical admission if red MEED features; family involvement negotiated with her
safetyNet: 999 for collapse, chest pain, palpitations or severe weakness; no exercise until assessed
GP review of results and ongoing physical monitoring until the specialist team takes over

pitfalls.intro: This station hides an eating disorder behind a request for iron. It is failed by accepting the anaemia story, by confronting her so bluntly that she shuts down, and by forgetting that the dizziness may be a medical emergency.

items.fail: Ordering an FBC and ferritin and offering iron.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” The history points to an eating disorder with possible medical instability.
items.fix: Ask about food, exercise, weight and periods, and say clearly: “I don’t think this is anaemia.”

items.fail: Recognising the eating disorder but only making a routine referral from a video call.
items.why: “Does not gather sufficient information to make a safe assessment.” MEED requires in-person observations; postural symptoms may mean she is unstable.
items.fix: Bring her in today for lying and standing observations, temperature, weight, bloods and ECG, and refer urgently.

items.fail: “You’re clearly too thin — you need to eat more.”
items.why: Confrontation increases defensiveness; she will minimise and may not return.
items.fix: Start from her words: “Tell me what a typical day of food and exercise looks like.”

items.fail: Missing the fear of losing control.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” Her resistance comes from fear, not stubbornness.
items.fix: “Food feels like the one thing you control. I won’t take decisions away from you — we’ll make them together.”

items.fail: Promising confidentiality, or telling her parents will be phoned without discussion.
items.why: Both fail the balance GMC 0–18 years requires between confidentiality and safety.
items.fix: Explain honestly that family must be involved, then negotiate who, when and how.

items.fail: Closing with “we’ll ring with the results” and no emergency advice.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting in a patient who is fainting.
items.fix: Name 999 triggers, pause exercise, confirm how she gets to the surgery today, and teach-back.

Cardiac red flags; a typical day of food and exercise in her words; feelings when she can’t train; weight change; periods; mood and self-harm.
Pressure to achieve; food as the one thing she controls; fear of being made to gain weight. Validate, don’t argue.
Name the eating disorder gently and its effect on her heart. Same-day in-person checks, bloods and ECG; immediate urgent referral; family involvement negotiated.
999 triggers, no exercise today, how she gets to the surgery. Teach-back of the plan.

wordPics.pass: Recognises a probable eating disorder; arranges in-person observations, bloods and ECG; refers to the eating disorder service; mentions family involvement; gives basic safety-netting.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: opens the subject through her own words without confrontation; validates the need for control; names the medical danger honestly; arranges same-day assessment with admission criteria in mind; negotiates how and when her family is told; confirms understanding with teach-back.

avoid.instead: “Tell me what a typical day of food and exercise looks like for you.”

avoid.instead: “I don’t think this is anaemia. Your body isn’t getting enough fuel, and I need to check your heart today.”

I think your eating and exercise have become an eating disorder, and it’s started to affect your heart and blood pressure.
SCA_MODELS.why: Names the probable eating disorder and its medical danger, gently

SCA_MODELS.text: I’m not ill. I’m just being healthy.

I can see why it feels that way — it started as trying to be healthy. But being healthy shouldn’t make you faint. This isn’t about blame or vanity; it’s an illness, it’s treatable, and people do recover. And I won’t make any decisions without you.
SCA_MODELS.why: Avoids argument, reframes as illness and restores some control

SCA_MODELS.text: …Okay.

Here’s what I’d like. I can’t check your heart properly over video, so I’d like you to come in today. We’ll check your pulse and blood pressure lying and standing, your temperature and weight, do a heart tracing and bloods for your salts and sugar. If anything is dangerous, you may need to be seen in hospital today.
SCA_MODELS.why: Same-day in-person MEED risk assessment, bloods and ECG

SCA_MODELS.text: Today? I’ve got revision.

I know exams matter a lot to you. Fainting could hurt you, and it will affect your revision far more than an hour here. I’ll also refer you urgently to the eating disorder team for young people — they’re specialists, and they aim to see urgent referrals within a week.
SCA_MODELS.why: Urgent CEDS referral in line with NICE NG69 and the waiting time standard

SCA_MODELS.text: Do my parents have to know?

Because this is affecting your physical safety, your family will need to be involved — the treatment that works best for people your age includes them. But we can decide together how, and what you’d like to say first. Would it help if I was there when you tell them?
SCA_MODELS.why: Honest about limits of confidentiality at 16, negotiated with her

SCA_MODELS.text: …Maybe. Mum, not Dad first.
That’s fine. Please come in this afternoon — can someone bring you? Until then, if you pass out, get chest pain, your heart races or you feel very weak, ring 999. Please don’t exercise today.
SCA_MODELS.why: Same-day attendance and explicit emergency triggers

SCA_MODELS.text: Before we finish, tell me in your own words what we’ve agreed.
Come in today for checks, bloods and a heart tracing. You’re referring me to a specialist team. We tell Mum together. 999 if I pass out or get chest pain.
Exactly. You came hoping for a quick fix, and I know this is harder to hear. You did the right thing coming, and you won’t be doing this alone.
SCA_MODELS.why: Closes with warmth and acknowledges the gap between wish and plan

SCA_STEM.name: Ivy
pmh: No significant past medical history recorded
SCA_STEM.recent: No recent consultations. No weight or blood results on record in the past year.
SCA_STEM.reason: Booked a video appointment herself: dizzy on standing, tired, feeling cold, and “fainting a bit” at school. Asking for iron tablets or a blood test.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG69 (eating disorders, 2017, updated 2020) · RCPsych CR233 Medical emergencies in eating disorders (MEED, 2022) · NHS England CYP eating disorder access and waiting time standard (2015) · GMC 0–18 years (2007)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Postural dizziness, faints, cold intolerance, amenorrhoea and rapid weight loss in a thin, driven teenager asking for iron is an eating disorder until proven otherwise — and a possible medical emergency. She needs an in-person physical risk assessment the same day and an immediate referral.

points.t: Restriction, calorie counting, hours of exercise, fear of weight gain, body-image distortion, rapid weight loss and amenorrhoea point to anorexia nervosa. Framing it as “healthy eating” is part of the illness, not evidence against it.

RCPsych MEED (CR233, 2022) covers all ages and uses a red, amber and green risk system: degree and rate of weight loss, heart rate, lying and standing blood pressure and pulse, temperature, hydration, the sit-up–squat–stand test, blood results and ECG. It advises that primary care assesses these in person and seeks collateral from family, as patients often minimise.

FBC, U&E, phosphate, magnesium, calcium, glucose, LFTs. NICE NG69: assess the need for ECG monitoring with rapid weight loss, excessive exercise, bradycardia, hypotension, electrolyte imbalance or muscular weakness — several of which apply. Normal bloods do not exclude danger.

NICE NG69: if an eating disorder is suspected after initial assessment, refer immediately to a community-based, age-appropriate eating disorder service. Do not use a single measure such as BMI or duration of illness to decide whether to offer treatment. One red or two or more amber MEED features need urgent same-day discussion with the acute paediatric and eating disorder teams; admit if she cannot be stabilised safely in the community.

NHS England standard (2015) for children and young people: treatment in line with NICE NG69 should start within 1 week for urgent cases and within 4 weeks for routine cases. Mark this referral urgent.

NICE NG69: consider anorexia-nervosa-focused family therapy for children and young people, with some appointments seen separately from family. Do not offer medication as the sole treatment. Family involvement is part of treatment, negotiated with her.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; took the faints seriously without accepting “just anaemia” and agreed a wider agenda.
Academic and parental pressure, perfectionism, need for control, mood and self-harm screen.
Picked up “eating healthily and exercising” and “I feel huge” and explored them without confrontation.
Idea (run down, anaemic), concern (being made to gain weight, losing control), expectation (iron or a blood test).
Same-day in-person lying and standing BP and pulse, temperature, weight, sit-up–squat–stand; FBC, U&E, phosphate, magnesium, glucose, LFTs; ECG (MEED, NICE NG69).
Anorexia nervosa vs anaemia, thyroid disease, coeliac disease and other causes of weight loss; cardiac causes of presyncope.
Asked about blackouts, chest pain and palpitations; recognised postural symptoms and rapid weight loss as possible medical instability.
Probable anorexia nervosa with possible medical instability, explained as an illness rather than a choice.
Same-day physical assessment with admission if red MEED features; immediate urgent referral to the community eating disorder service.
Low mood screened; exam pressure acknowledged; family involvement negotiated; exercise paused today.
999 for collapse, chest pain, palpitations or weakness; seen today; review after results and once the team is involved.

social.t: High academic and parental expectations often sit behind restriction as a means of control. Acknowledge exams as important to her while making clear that her safety comes first.
Family-based treatment is central for adolescents (NICE NG69). She may want one parent told first; honouring that preference where safe keeps her engaged.

legal.t: At 16 she is presumed to have capacity (Mental Capacity Act 2005) and can consent to treatment (Family Law Reform Act 1969, s8). Anorexia can impair capacity for decisions about food and weight; assess capacity for the specific decision.

GMC 0–18 years: information can be shared without consent where necessary to protect a young person from risk of death or serious harm. A medically unstable eating disorder can meet this threshold; involve her in how it is done.
If illness affects her exams, her school can apply for access arrangements or special consideration through the exam boards’ JCQ process.

professional.t: MEED advises in-person physical assessment in primary care. A video consultation can open the subject but cannot measure postural observations; arrange a same-day face-to-face review (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024: recognise the limits of the consultation).
Record the history, observations, MEED risk features, the referral and its urgency, and the confidentiality discussion.

community.t: Beat (UK eating disorder charity) for Ivy and her family; school pastoral team or school nurse, with her agreement; the community eating disorder service’s family support.

redFlags: Syncope, chest pain, palpitations or muscle weakness — urgent assessment
Rapid weight loss, bradycardia, postural drop, low temperature, failed sit-up–squat–stand — MEED red or amber features
Self-harm or suicidal thoughts; purging or laxative use
psychosocial: Perfectionism and parental expectations; top sets; A-levels
Food and exercise as the one area she controls
Shame and fear of being made to gain weight
ice: Idea: “I’m run down with exams — maybe anaemic.”
Concern: being made to gain weight and losing control
Expectation: iron tablets or a blood test

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Probable anorexia nervosa (restriction, compulsive exercise, fear of weight gain, body-image distortion, rapid weight loss, 4 months’ amenorrhoea) with symptoms suggesting medical instability (postural presyncope, cold intolerance). Needs same-day in-person physical risk assessment.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Your body isn’t getting enough fuel for what you’re asking of it, so it’s slowing things down — that’s why you’re cold, your periods stopped and you go grey when you stand. That’s an eating disorder. It’s an illness, not a choice, and it can be treated.”

management.reflectIce: “You were hoping this was anaemia, and you’re frightened of being made to gain weight and losing control. I won’t make decisions without you, but I do need to keep you safe.”
management.psychosocial: Validate the pressure and need for control; avoid food and weight arguments; negotiate which parent is told first and how; involve school only with her agreement.
sharedPlan: Same-day in-person observations (lying and standing BP and pulse, temperature, weight, sit-up–squat–stand), bloods and ECG (MEED, NICE NG69)
Immediate urgent referral to the community eating disorder service (NICE NG69; NHS England standard, urgent within 1 week)
Same-day medical admission if red MEED features; family involvement negotiated with her
safetyNet: 999 for collapse, chest pain, palpitations or severe weakness; no exercise until assessed
GP review of results and ongoing physical monitoring until the specialist team takes over

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station hides an eating disorder behind a request for iron. It is failed by accepting the anaemia story, by confronting her so bluntly that she shuts down, and by forgetting that the dizziness may be a medical emergency.

items.fail: Ordering an FBC and ferritin and offering iron.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” The history points to an eating disorder with possible medical instability.
items.fix: Ask about food, exercise, weight and periods, and say clearly: “I don’t think this is anaemia.”

items.fail: Recognising the eating disorder but only making a routine referral from a video call.
items.why: “Does not gather sufficient information to make a safe assessment.” MEED requires in-person observations; postural symptoms may mean she is unstable.
items.fix: Bring her in today for lying and standing observations, temperature, weight, bloods and ECG, and refer urgently.

items.fail: “You’re clearly too thin — you need to eat more.”
items.why: Confrontation increases defensiveness; she will minimise and may not return.
items.fix: Start from her words: “Tell me what a typical day of food and exercise looks like.”

items.fail: Missing the fear of losing control.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” Her resistance comes from fear, not stubbornness.
items.fix: “Food feels like the one thing you control. I won’t take decisions away from you — we’ll make them together.”

items.fail: Promising confidentiality, or telling her parents will be phoned without discussion.
items.why: Both fail the balance GMC 0–18 years requires between confidentiality and safety.
items.fix: Explain honestly that family must be involved, then negotiate who, when and how.

items.fail: Closing with “we’ll ring with the results” and no emergency advice.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting in a patient who is fainting.
items.fix: Name 999 triggers, pause exercise, confirm how she gets to the surgery today, and teach-back.
